paper_title: Biophilic Design and Restorative Effects: A Neuropsychological Study of Healthy Indoor Workspaces in Urban Contexts
venue: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
abstract: The rapid increases in urbanization and time spent in built indoor environments have sparked significant concerns about their impact on human health and well-being. People who spend long hours in enclosed and highly artificial settings, such as hospital workers, are especially vulnerable to environmental stressors. This study examined whether applying biophilic (i.e., human tendency to connect with nature and other lifeforms) spatial design within hospital spaces could provide restorative benefits for nurses working in high-stress environments. Twenty-one nurses participated in this study, staying under two different conditions for 10 min: a control room with plain white walls and a biophilic space where the walls were entirely covered with vegetation. During the sessions, functional near-infrared spectroscopy was used to measure hemodynamic responses in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC). Additionally, standardized self-report questionnaires were used to analyze the level of perceived restorativeness, affective states, mood, and anxiety. Results showed that exposure to the biophilic space significantly reduced oxyhemoglobin (oxy-Hb) concentrations in the DLPFC, reflecting relief from cognitive-emotional overload and enhanced neural stabilization. Psychological measures further indicated decreases in fatigue, depression, and anxiety, alongside increases in vigor, attentiveness, and perceived restorativeness in biophilic space. These findings demonstrate that even brief exposure to a biophilically designed indoor environment can produce neuropsychologically restorative effects, suggesting biophilic interventions as sustainable, effective strategies for healthier workplaces and urban environments.
methodology: This study employed a within-subject repeated-measures design with randomized order of conditions. Participants were exposed to two different indoor settings (control vs. biophilic) for 10 minutes each, with a 3-minute stabilization period between conditions. Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) was used to measure hemodynamic responses (oxyhemoglobin concentrations) in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC). Psychological states were assessed using self-report questionnaires: Perceived Restorativeness Scale (PRS), Zuckerman Inventory of Personal Reaction Scale (ZIPERS), Profile of Mood States-Brief (POMS), and State-Trait Anxiety Inventory (STAI). Data analysis involved paired t-tests for fNIRS data and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests for psychological data.
sample: 21 nurses (mean age: 35.0 ± 7.9 years) working in a national hospital in Cheon-An City, South Korea. Participants were adults without a history of neuropsychiatric or cardiovascular disorders.

manipulated_features.description: A room with plain white walls, same flooring material as the biophilic space, cleared of all furniture and decorative elements. Maintained at 25.9 ± 0.6 °C, 61.5 ± 4.3% humidity, and 373.0 ± 61.1 lx illuminance.

A naturalized space where walls were entirely covered with vegetation, providing a total green area of 21 m². 10 species of foliage plants were cultivated in individual pots and arranged to uniformly cover the wall surface. Maintained at 25.9 ± 0.6 °C, 61.5 ± 4.3% humidity, and 373.0 ± 61.1 lx illuminance.

outcomes: Oxyhemoglobin (oxy-Hb) concentrations in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) (neurophysiological)
Perceived Restorativeness Scale (PRS) total score and subdomains (being away, fascination, coherence, compatibility) (psychological)
Zuckerman Inventory of Personal Reaction Scale (ZIPERS) subscales (positive affect, attentiveness, fear, anger, sadness) (psychological)
Profile of Mood States-Brief (POMS) subscales (vigor, fatigue, depression) (psychological)
key_findings: Exposure to the biophilic space significantly reduced oxyhemoglobin (oxy-Hb) concentrations in the DLPFC compared to the control condition (Control: -0.030 ± 0.001 µmol/L; Biophilic space: -0.066 ± 0.001 µmol/L, p < 0.001), reflecting a reduction of over 50%.
Perceived Restorativeness Scale (PRS) total scores were significantly higher in the biophilic space (98.52 ± 4.07) compared to the control (53.62 ± 3.98, p < 0.01).

PRS subscales showed significant increases in biophilic space: Being away (Biophilic: 12.24 ± 0.80 vs. Control: 6.62 ± 0.96, p < 0.01), Fascination (Biophilic: 27.38 ± 1.61 vs. Control: 9.48 ± 1.76, p < 0.01), Coherence (Biophilic: 29.81 ± 1.10 vs. Control: 25.05 ± 1.05, p < 0.01), and Compatibility (Biophilic: 29.10 ± 1.88 vs. Control: 12.48 ± 1.89, p < 0.01).

Zuckerman Inventory of Personal Reaction Scale (ZIPERS) showed significantly higher positive affect (Biophilic: 13.29 ± 0.47 vs. Control: 10.19 ± 0.54, p < 0.01) and attentiveness (Biophilic: 7.38 ± 0.27 vs. Control: 5.24 ± 0.22, p < 0.01) in the biophilic space.
ZIPERS also showed significantly lower fear in the biophilic space (Biophilic: 4.95 ± 0.37 vs. Control: 6.00 ± 0.55, p < 0.01).

Profile of Mood States-Brief (POMS) indicated significantly higher vigor (Biophilic: 7.10 ± 1.06 vs. Control: 2.00 ± 0.79, p < 0.01) and significantly lower fatigue (Biophilic: 2.71 ± 0.65 vs. Control: 5.48 ± 0.62, p < 0.01) and depression (Biophilic: 1.19 ± 0.35 vs. Control: 3.67 ± 0.62, p < 0.01) in the biophilic space.
State-Trait Anxiety Inventory (STAI) scores were significantly decreased in the biophilic space (Biophilic: 37.14 ± 1.72 vs. Control: 44.95 ± 1.91, p < 0.01).
mechanisms: Reduced DLPFC activation reflects relief from cognitive-emotional overload and enhanced neural stabilization.
Decreased DLPFC activity suggests neurochemical rebalancing through neurotransmitters such as norepinephrine, dopamine, and acetylcholine, facilitating cortical stabilization.
Temporal variations in hemodynamic patterns may represent adaptive neuroplastic processes by which the brain transitions into more efficient states.
Nature mitigates neurophysiological stress responses, potentially by reducing amygdala activity.
Natural environments reduce cognitive load and promote attentional restoration, consistent with Attention Restoration Theory.
limitations: Relatively small sample size (21 participants) restricts generalizability.
Short-term exposure period (10 min) limits the assessment of long-term biophilic effects.
Possibility of self-selection bias due to voluntary participation.
The control condition (plain white wall) might be an overly simplified contrast to a typical indoor environment, potentially overstating the effects.

The study focused on a single biophilic attribute (greenery exposure), not exploring other sensory-integrated attributes (e.g., water, view, shelter, biodiversity, light, scent, sound) or compositional variations.
design_implications: Biophilic design elements in artificial hospital environments can alleviate neurophysiological stress, enhance emotional recovery, and reduce occupational strain among healthcare professionals.
Introducing biophilic elements into accessible restorative spaces (e.g., for 10-minute breaks) is a practical and compatible environmental strategy for high-stress occupations.

The findings provide a valuable foundation for the standardized application of biophilic design in hospital architecture and interior planning to create healthier and more restorative healthcare environments.

Embedding restorative natural elements into built environments can serve as a cost-effective, sustainable intervention to enhance public health, improve resilience to stress, and strengthen the overall livability of cities.

environmental_features: indoor workspace with biophilic design elements (e.g., plants, natural light simulation, natural materials, nature-themed artwork/views)
indoor workspace with conventional design (control condition, e.g., standard office decor, urban views or no specific view)

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Biophilic design elements in indoor workspaces can facilitate psychological restoration by engaging involuntary attention and reducing mental fatigue, thereby improving cognitive function.

instruments_used.name: N-back task
instruments_used.description: A continuous performance task used to measure working memory capacity.

instruments_used.name: Stroop task
instruments_used.description: A task measuring reaction time and accuracy in naming the color of words, often conflicting with the word itself.

instruments_used.name: Perceived Restorativeness Scale (PRS)
instruments_used.description: A self-report questionnaire assessing the restorative quality of an environment based on ART components (being away, fascination, extent, compatibility).

instruments_used.name: Positive and Negative Affect Schedule (PANAS)
instruments_used.description: A 20-item self-report questionnaire measuring current positive and negative mood states.

instruments_used.name: Heart Rate Variability (HRV)
instruments_used.construct: physiological stress, autonomic nervous system activity
instruments_used.description: Measurement of the variation in the time interval between heartbeats, used as an indicator of stress and relaxation.

mechanism_chain.description: Exposure to biophilic design elements leads to increased feelings of fascination and being away, which in turn reduces mental fatigue and stress, ultimately improving cognitive performance and well-being.
